extracted.intended_audience: law students, legal researchers, and practitioners interested in California administrative rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: A concise guide to the procedural and substantive requirements California agencies must follow when adopting regulations through notice-and-comment rulemaking, including notice contents, supporting documents (ISOR/FSOR), simplified procedures, and OAL oversight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice publication in the Notice Register (Z Register)
rubrics_metrics.description: The agency publishes a notice of the proposed regulation in the Notice Register (also nicknamed the Z Register).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The notice is the formal public announcement of the proposal and serves as the starting point for the public participation process. It must accompany other required disclosure elements (informative digest, where to obtain proposed text and ISOR, comment/hearing info).

rubrics_metrics.name: Informative digest requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The notice must include an informative digest that explains in plain English what the regulation does, why it is being made, and its anticipated impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Digest should be intelligible to a non-specialist (plain English) and summarize the regulation's purpose and expected effects; it is meant to inform the public and facilitate meaningful comment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Initial Statement of Reasons (ISOR) availability
rubrics_metrics.description: The notice must explain where to obtain the proposed text of the regulation and the initial statement of reasons (ISOR), a more detailed explanation of why the regulation is being made and its anticipated impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ISOR provides the substantive factual and legal justification for the rulemaking; the notice must direct readers to the ISOR so commenters can evaluate the agency's rationale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public comment submission and hearing information
rubrics_metrics.description: The notice must include information on where to submit comments on the regulation, including the name and contact information for an agency staff member and the time and location of any public hearings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clear contact details and hearing logistics ensure the public can participate; omission or inadequate detail can undermine the validity of the notice and participation opportunities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to publish notice of changes and allow additional comment when regulation is changed after comments
rubrics_metrics.description: If the agency decides to change the regulation in response to public comments, the agency must publish a notice of the changes and provide the public with additional time to submit comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Substantive post-comment changes trigger further notice-and-comment opportunity so the public can respond to revised language; failure to do so risks procedural challenge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Final Statement of Reasons (FSOR) requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Once the agency is satisfied with the regulation, the agency updates the informative digest and prepares a Final Statement of Reasons (FSOR) that updates the information in the ISOR, summarizes and responds to public comments, and provides additional specified information on the regulation's anticipated impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: FSOR documents the agency's final rationale, how it addressed comments, and any new impact analysis; it is the administrative record explaining adoption decisions and is important for judicial review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication of final notice and updating of the California Code of Regulations
rubrics_metrics.description: The Notice Register publishes a final notice of the regulation's adoption and the final text of the regulation is mailed out in the weekly Register; the California Code of Regulations (CCR) is published in loose leaf binders and updated by replacing outdated pages with new ones from the Register.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Final publication procedures produce the official, citable regulatory text; understanding Register/CCR update mechanics is important for locating current regulatory language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emergency regulation process and time limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Emergency regulations follow a simplified process and remain in effect for 180 days plus up to two 90-day extensions while the agency completes the full rulemaking process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emergency rulemaking allows agencies to act quickly when necessary, but time limits require agencies to later complete standard notice-and-comment procedures or the emergency rule will expire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Changes without regulatory effect (non-substantive amendments)
rubrics_metrics.description: Changes without regulatory effect, such as fixing typos or updating citations to regulations and statutes that have moved, are made without any formal process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Non-substantive edits that do not alter rights/obligations can be processed more simply; agencies should ensure changes truly have no regulatory effect to avoid bypassing required procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Office of Administrative Law (OAL) oversight responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: The Office of Administrative Law (OAL) is responsible for making sure that other agencies follow the rulemaking process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OAL reviews agency rulemaking for compliance with procedural norms and legal standards before registering regulations; OAL functions as a gatekeeper to ensure processes such as notice and adequate comment opportunities were observed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Underground regulation determinations by OAL
rubrics_metrics.description: OAL may issue underground regulation determinations, determining that a rule the agency is enforcing informally is actually a regulation and must be either abandoned or passed formally through notice-and-comment rulemaking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These determinations prevent agencies from evading formal rulemaking by creating binding rules through informal practices; agencies found to have underground regulations must either stop informal enforcement or undertake formal rulemaking.

rubrics_metrics.name: OAL disapproval decisions and grounds (e.g., inadequate time for public comment)
rubrics_metrics.description: OAL may issue disapproval decisions, rejecting regulations if the agency has failed to properly follow the process, such as by allowing inadequate time for public comment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disapproval can nullify an adopted regulation for procedural defects; common grounds include insufficient notice, inadequate comment period, or failure to provide required supporting documents (ISOR/FSOR).
